standard.title: Code of Practice for Photogeological Interpretation and Mapping of River Valley Project Sites (नदी घाटी परियोजना स्थलों के फोटो-भूवैज्ञानिक व्याख्या और मानचित्रण की रीति संहिता)
standard.description: This standard specifies standard guidelines, recommended scale criteria, mapping workflows, and field verification procedures for using aerial photography and stereoscopic interpretation to map geological, morphological, and structural features of river valley project sites, providing rapid, economical, and dependable ground evaluations prior to construction.
standard.scope: This standard specifies standard guidelines, recommended scale criteria, mapping workflows, and field verification procedures for using aerial photography and stereoscopic interpretation to map geological, morphological, and structural features of river valley project sites, providing rapid, economical, and dependable ground evaluations prior to construction.

certification.description: Voluntary Code of Practice. Since IS 10290:1982 is an engineering guideline and operational code of practice for geological exploration and photogeological mapping rather than a direct consumer product, it does not carry an individual mandatory BIS 'ISI Mark' product stamp. However, compliance with its recommended photograph scales, contour ranges, operational flow sequences, and site suitability guidelines is strictly mandated by the Central Water Commission (CWC), Geological Survey of India (GSI), and state water resources departments when preparing Detailed Project Reports (DPRs), tender packages, and environmental clearances for dam, tunnel, and powerhouse sites across India. Precious metal hallmarking is completely inapplicable.
requirements:
Specifies three mandatory physical assets required to construct an interpreted photogeological map:
a) High-quality aerial photographs;
b) A stereoscope; and
c) Topographic base maps with contours.
The photo-interpreted map represents a preliminary stage and MUST be field checked and verified on-ground to correct interpretations, add on-site details, and prepare the final geological profiles.

Specifies contour intervals matching the selected photographic and mapping scale, ranging from fine details of 1 m to 5 m (for 1 : 5 000 scale maps) up to 5 m to 20 m (for 1 : 25 000 scale feasibility maps) to ensure adequate vertical and topographic relief resolution.

Identifies that damage to civil structures is maximum under two geologically mapped conditions:
a) Siting structures astride or too close to a tectonic feature (such as active faults, shear zones, or joints) activated during an earthquake; or
b) Siting structures on deep alluvial deposits or unconsolidated materials (which suffer far more severe damage than bedrock during seismic events). Structures must be strategically moved to bedrock or safer strata as mapped.

Powerhouse site photogeological mapping requires the same comprehensive steps as a dam site, but must additionally study aerial photographs for slope stability and mapping the orientation of joints within the local rock mass.

Tunnel alignments require careful planning to avoid difficult and hazardous geological conditions. Photogeological interpretation is established as an essential tool to compare DESIGN and COST of tunnel excavation across several considered routes.
